summary: The bill imposes an annual tax on the net assets of individuals and certain trusts above $50 million (2% between $50 million and $1 billion, and 3% above that, or 6% if paired with universal health coverage legislation), with rules for asset valuation, information reporting, audits, and IRS funding.

scores.thoughts: Section 4 of the bill authorizes $100 billion in new appropriations for the IRS (enforcement, taxpayer services, and modernization) over fiscal years 2027-2037. This is a direct, substantial expansion of federal spending, even though the primary purpose of the legislation is revenue-raising. The magnitude is medium-to-large because the spending authorization is explicit and sizable.

The entire bill creates a new annual wealth tax (Subtitle B-1) on the net value of assets above $50 million, with rates of 2% and 3% (or 6% under certain conditions). This is a direct, high-rate tax increase targeted at ultra-wealthy individuals. The legislation is almost entirely about imposing this new tax.

Section 2901(c) provides that the top marginal rate rises from 3% to 6% only if Congress later enacts legislation creating a universal public health insurance program that bars private duplicate coverage. This is merely a conditional trigger, not an actual healthcare policy change, so the connection is weak and indirect.
